difficultyRationale: A practical performance decision candidates should recognize even without memorizing the exact Spring Data projection mechanics.
prompt: A `GET /employees/summary` endpoint only needs `id`, `fullName`, and `departmentName` for a list of 10,000 employees, but the `Employee` entity has 30 columns including a large `resume` TEXT field and a `photo` BLOB field. A repository method is declared as `List<EmployeeSummary> findAllProjectedBy()`, where `EmployeeSummary` is an interface exposing only those three accessor methods. Why does using this projection matter here?
explanation: An interface-based (or DTO) projection lets Spring Data build a query that selects only the columns the projection actually needs, so the heavy `resume` and `photo` columns are never read off the database or materialized into Java objects for any of the 10,000 rows — unlike returning `List<Employee>`, which hydrates every mapped column of every row whether the caller needs it or not.

options.text: An interface-based (or DTO) projection can be backed by a query selecting only id, fullName, and departmentName, avoiding the cost of reading and materializing the BLOB/TEXT columns and the rest of the entity for all 10,000 rows, instead of hydrating a full Employee object for each one.
options.explanation: Correct. The projection narrows what the database actually has to return and what the JVM has to materialize, which matters a lot at 10,000 rows when the skipped columns are large.

options.text: Projections are purely a compile-time convenience on the repository interface; at runtime Spring Data still loads the complete Employee entity for every matching row and simply hides the unused getters from the object it hands back to the caller.
options.explanation: Spring Data generates a query shaped around the projection's declared properties rather than always loading the full entity first; if that were true, projections would offer no actual performance benefit over returning entities, which defeats their main purpose.

options.text: Interface-based projections only work when the projection interface is declared in the exact same Java package as the entity class; EmployeeSummary would have to live alongside Employee for Spring Data to recognize it as a valid projection at all.
options.explanation: There's no such same-package requirement; Spring Data recognizes a projection interface by its method signatures matching the source properties, and it can live in any package, such as a dedicated DTO or projection package.

options.text: Using a projection requires Hibernate's second-level cache to already be enabled and properly configured for the Employee entity ahead of time; without an active second-level cache region defined for it, calling findAllProjectedBy() throws a configuration exception during repository initialization at application startup.
options.explanation: Projections have nothing to do with second-level caching; they work against a plain query result set and don't require, or even interact directly with, the entity's cache configuration.
